e-8224.knowledge_point: Identifying Sets That Are Not Vector Spaces
e-8224.problem:
Let $V$ be the set of all real polynomials of degree exactly $3$, equipped with the usual addition and scalar multiplication operations. Complete the following sentence:

*$V$ is **not** a vector space because $\textrm{_________}\,.$*

- the sum of two polynomials of degree $3$ may not be a polynomial of degree $3$

- $V$ does not contain the polynomial $-p(x)$ for every $p(x) \in V$

- addition of polynomials is not commutative
e-8224.worked_solution:
The correct answer  is as follows:

*$V$ is **not** a vector space because **the sum of two polynomials of degree $3$ may not be a polynomial of degree $3$.** *

For instance, if $p(x) = 1 +x^3$ and $q(x) = 1-x^3$, then $p(x)$ and $q(x)$ are in $V.$ However  

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x)+q(x) & =(1+{x}^{3})+(1-{x}^{3}) \\  & =2\notin V.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand:

- Addition of polynomials is commutative.

- For any polynomial $p(x)$ of degree $3$, the corresponding negative polynomial $-p(x)$ also has degree $3.$

e-4792.problem:
From top to bottom, fill in the blanks and hence complete the proof of the following statement using the axioms $[\textrm A1] - [\textrm A8]$ given below.

*Statement: *

*If $\mathbf{w}$ is a vector such that $\mathbf{w}+\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{w}$, then $\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{0}.$* 

*Proof:*

$$
\begin{aligned}w+w & =w &  & [\,\text{given}\,] \\ (w+w)+(-w) & =w+(-w) &  & [\,\text{add [math]-\mathbf{w}[/math] to both sides}\,] \\ w+(w+(-w)) & =w+(-w) &  & [\,\text{axiom __}\,\,] \\ w+0 & =0 &  & [\,\text{axiom A4}\,] \\ w & =0 &  & [\,\text{axiom __}\,\,]\end{aligned}
$$

The axioms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{[A1]}:x+y=y+x & \text{[A5]}:1\cdot x=x \\ \text{[A2]}:(x+y)+z=x+(y+z) & \text{[A6]}:\alpha (\beta x)=(\alpha \beta )x \\ \text{[A3]}:x+0=x & \text{[A7]}:(\alpha +\beta )x=\alpha x+\beta x \\ \text{[A4]}:x+(-x)=0 & \text{[A8]}:\alpha (x+y)=\alpha x+\alpha y\end{aligned}
$$

Using the axioms of a vector space, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}w+w & =w &  & [\,\text{given}\,] \\ (w+w)+(-w) & =w+(-w) &  & [\,\text{add [math]-\mathbf{w}[/math] to both sides}\,] \\ w+(w+(-w)) & =w+(-w) &  & [\,\text{axiom [math]{\color{blue}\text{A2}}[/math]}\,] \\ w+0 & =0 &  & [\,\text{axiom A4}\,] \\ w & =0 &  & [\,\text{axiom [math]{\color{blue}\text{A3}}[/math]}\,]\end{aligned}

*$Y$ is **not** a vector space (with respect to the usual component-wise addition and scalar multiplication in ${R}^{2}$) because **multiplication of $(x,y)\in Y$ by a scalar is not closed.** *

- Addition in $Y$ is associative. $\,✓$

From top to bottom, fill in the blanks and hence complete the proof of the following statement using the axioms $[\text{A}1]-[\text{A}8]$ given below.

*Statement: *

*If $u$ and $v$ are vectors such that $u+x=v+x$ for some $x\in V,$ then $u=v.$*

*Proof:*

$$
\begin{aligned}u+x & =v+x &  & [\,\text{given}\,] \\ (u+x)+(-x) & =(v+x)+(-x) &  & [\,\text{add }-x\text{ to both sides}\,] \\ u+(x+(-x)) & =v+(x+(-x)) &  & [\,\text{axiom A2}\,] \\ u+0 & =v+0 &  & [\,\text{axiom __}\,\,] \\ u & =v &  & [\,\text{axiom __}\,\,]\end{aligned}
$$

The axioms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{[A1]}:x+y=y+x & \text{[A5]}:1\cdot x=x \\ \text{[A2]}:(x+y)+z=x+(y+z) & \text{[A6]}:\alpha (\beta x)=(\alpha \beta )x \\ \text{[A3]}:x+0=x & \text{[A7]}:(\alpha +\beta )x=\alpha x+\beta x \\ \text{[A4]}:x+(-x)=0 & \text{[A8]}:\alpha (x+y)=\alpha x+\alpha y\end{aligned}
$$
